name: Cross Coloring
description: There is a sheet of paper that can be represented with a grid of size $$$n \times m$$$: $$$n$$$ rows and $$$m$$$ columns of cells. All cells are colored in white initially. $$$q$$$ operations have been applied to the sheet. The $$$i$$$-th of them can be described as follows: $$$x_i$$$ $$$y_i$$$ — choose one of $$$k$$$ non-white colors and color the entire row $$$x_i$$$ and the entire column $$$y_i$$$ in it. The new color is applied to each cell, regardless of whether the cell was colored before the operation. The sheet after applying all $$$q$$$ operations is called a coloring. Two colorings are different if there exists at least one cell that is colored in different colors. How many different colorings are there? Print the number modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of testcases. The first line of the testcase contains four integers $$$n, m, k$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le n, m, k, q \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the size of the sheet, the number of non-white colors and the number of operations. The $$$i$$$-th of the following $$$q$$$ lines contains a description of the $$$i$$$-th operation — two integers $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i \le n$$$; $$$1 \le y_i \le m$$$) — the row and the column the operation is applied to. The sum of $$$q$$$ over all testcases doesn't exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each testcase, print a single integer — the number of different colorings modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1644D — Cross Coloring [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
